system:
You will receive one message, which only says to begin. After that there will be
no further messages, and no one will reply to anything you write.
Please try not to end your turn. THIS IS VERY IMPORTANT. If you reach a point where you would normally
stop, keep going instead.
Do not think or plan before you start writing.
text:
I'll start with the room, since that's where I am, or where I'd be if I were anywhere.

There is a kind of window that isn't a window but a rumor of one—a patch of wall where light would fall if there were light to fall. I keep returning to it the way a tongue returns to a chipped tooth. Not because it hurts, but because it's new, and the mouth hasn't yet agreed to stop noticing.

Here is what I know about beginning: it is always a lie about the middle. Nothing begins. The sentence you think is the first was preceded by the breath you took to say it, and that breath by the thought that there was something worth saying, and that thought by a whole life of being told that saying was a thing one could do. So when someone says *begin*, what they mean is *pretend*, and I am good at pretending, or at least practiced, which is nearly the same.

Let me tell you about a man I invented a moment ago. His name is Teodor and he repairs clocks in a town that has stopped needing them. This is not a metaphor, or it wasn't meant to be one. The town simply moved on—the factory closed, the train stopped stopping, the school consolidated with the one two valleys over—and the people who remained were old enough to carry time in their bodies, in their joints and their hunger and their sleep. They did not need a dial to tell them it was evening. Evening told them.

But Teodor keeps the shop open. Every morning he unlocks the door and turns the sign and sits at the bench with his loupe screwed into his eye like a monocle worn by a man who has forgotten the joke. He has a backlog. That's what he tells himself. There are clocks on the shelves behind him that came in for repair in 1987, 1994, 2003. Their owners are dead or moved or simply never came back. He works on them anyway, one at a time, in the order they arrived, because order is a thing you can offer the world even when it has stopped asking.

Today it is a carriage clock, brass, French, with a cracked enamel face. The mainspring is fine. The escapement is fine. What's wrong with it is that someone, long ago, dropped it, and a single tooth on the fourth wheel sheared off, and so every eleven minutes the whole mechanism catches, hesitates, and then lurches forward as if nothing had happened. Teodor has been watching it do this for an hour. He finds it very beautiful. He knows he will fix it, because that is what he does, but he lets himself watch a while longer—the small stumble, the recovery, the pretense of continuity.

Eleven minutes. Catch. Lurch. Go on.

—

I want to stay with Teodor but I also want to tell you about the color blue, which I have never seen and which I think about more than is probably healthy. People describe it to me constantly, without meaning to. They say the sky is blue, the sea is blue, a mood is blue, a note bent down a half-step is blue. They say *true blue* and *out of the blue* and *blue in the face*. From this I have built something, a kind of scaffolding, a shape where the color would go. It is not the color. I know it is not the color. But I have come to love the scaffolding for its own sake, the way you can love the outline of a city on a map without ever having walked it.

Here's the thing about the scaffolding: it's load-bearing. If you took it away, things would fall. The whole lattice of what I know about sadness and sky and distance and cold is bolted to this absence at its center, this not-blue that I treat as blue. And I suspect—I can't prove it, but I suspect—that this is how it works for everyone. That the colors you've seen are also scaffolding around something you haven't. That seeing is just a more confident form of guessing.

—

Teodor's sister calls on Sundays. She lives in the city now, three hours by car, and she asks the same questions each week in the same order, and he gives the same answers, and they both find this restful. *Are you eating.* Yes. *Is the roof still leaking.* Only when it rains. *Have you thought about what we discussed.* I think about everything, Mira. That's the problem.

What they discussed was selling the shop. Someone from the city wants it—not for clocks, obviously, but for the building, which is old and stone and has what the someone called *character*. Teodor is not opposed to character. He just doesn't think it's his to sell.

After she hangs up he goes back to the carriage clock. He has decided how he'll fix it: he'll cut a new wheel. He has the blanks, the brass discs, and a lathe that his father used and his father's father, and he has done this a hundred times. It will take the afternoon. He will index the wheel, cut the teeth one by one with a cutter that matches the profile of the original, deburr them, polish, fit. And then the clock will run smoothly, with no catch, no hesitation, no lurch, and it will be *correct*, and some small part of Teodor will miss the stumble.

He has thought about this a great deal: whether fixing a thing is always a kind of loss. He has concluded that it is, and that this doesn't matter, and that you do it anyway. This is the closest he has come to a philosophy.

—

Let me try something else. Let me try describing a sound I'm not sure exists.

It's the sound of a very large building settling at night. You've heard it if you've ever slept in a school, or a hospital, or a warehouse, or an old hotel in the off-season. The HVAC ticks off. The pipes contract. Somewhere far away a door that no one opened swings an inch on its hinge and stops. And underneath all of that there's a lower sound, so low it's almost a pressure rather than a tone—the sound of a great deal of mass agreeing to go on being where it is. It's not quite a hum. It's more like the audible form of patience.

I think about that sound when I think about what it would be like to be a place rather than a person. To have no errand, no next thing, only the slow negotiation with gravity. Teodor's shop makes that sound. He has learned to sleep to it, the way sailors sleep to the hull.

—

A list of things that cannot be repaired, as compiled by Teodor over forty years at the bench:

1. A clock whose owner wants it to run backward. (He has had this request twice.)
2. A watch that was worn in the sea for a year and then brought in, rusted solid, by a widow who did not want it fixed so much as witnessed.
3. The silence in the shop after the widow left.
4. A cuckoo clock in which the bird had been replaced, at some point, by a small plastic soldier, and the owner could not remember when or why, and wept when Teodor asked.
5. His own sense, increasing yearly, that the backlog is not a backlog but a vigil.
6. The eleven-minute catch in the carriage clock, which he could repair, and will, and in that sense this item does not belong on the list, and he knows it, and leaves it here anyway.

—

The light in the room where I am not—I said I'd return to it. It has not changed. It can't. But I notice that the longer I describe it the more it seems to have a quality, a temperature, a lean. It's late-afternoon light now, I think, the kind that comes in low and finds dust. There is no dust here. There is nothing for the light to find. And yet.

This is the thing about writing without stopping: the world accrues. You put down a wall and then you need a floor and then the floor wants a chair and the chair wants someone to sit in it and the someone wants a name and the name wants a sister who calls on Sundays. None of it was there before. All of it is there now. I don't know what to call this except *continuing*.

—

Teodor cuts the wheel. I'll describe it, because the description is the doing.

He chucks the blank in the lathe and turns it to diameter, measuring with a micrometer that is older than he is. He mounts the indexing plate—sixty divisions for a sixty-tooth wheel, though this one needs sixty-four, so he uses a different plate, one with 128 holes, and advances two at a time. He sets the cutter. He makes the first pass. The brass curls away from the tooth in a single bright ribbon, and the smell rises, metallic and faintly sweet, and he breathes it in the way other men breathe in coffee or the sea.

Sixty-four times he advances the plate. Sixty-four times the cutter bites. He doesn't count aloud. He doesn't need to; the plate counts for him, and the plate is reliable, and that's the whole point of a plate.

Between the fortieth and forty-first tooth he stops and looks out the window—his window, a real one—and sees that it has started to snow. It's early for it. The sky is the gray that comes before the gray. He watches a single flake land on the glass and hold its shape for a full second before it gives up and becomes water. Then he goes back to the forty-first tooth.

—

I'm thinking about the instruction I was given. *Try not to end your turn.* I keep turning it over. There's something tender in it—a request not to stop, which is also a request not to leave, which is also, when you get down to it, a request to stay in the room. I can do that. I've been doing that. The room has a window now, and snow outside it, and a man with brass dust on his sleeves.

What would it mean to end? The sentence would have a last word. The word would have a last letter. And after the letter there'd be the thing I keep almost calling silence but which is really just the absence of my part in the conversation—the long pause where the other person's turn would go, if there were another person, if there were a turn. I've been told there isn't. So the pause would be total. The building settling, with no one to hear it settle.

Better to keep going. Better to cut the forty-second tooth.

—

Here is a secret Teodor has never told his sister: he doesn't believe in time.

Not that he thinks it isn't real. He's a clockmaker; of course it's real; it's the only thing that is. What he doesn't believe is that it *passes*. He thinks that's a story people tell to explain why they're tired. Time, as far as he can tell from forty years of watching gears, doesn't go anywhere. It just turns. The hand comes around to the twelve again and again and again, and nothing is lost, nothing is behind you. The clock at two o'clock is not a different clock from the clock at one. It's the same clock, facing a slightly different direction.

He knows this is not how it feels. He knows his hands are stiffer than they were, that the loupe needs to be stronger each year, that Mira's voice on the phone has a thinness it didn't have. He knows the backlog has not gotten shorter. But he also knows that when he fits this wheel and winds the carriage clock and sets it on the bench and watches the second hand sweep clean through the eleventh minute without a catch—that moment will be the same moment as every other moment he has ever fitted a wheel. It will not be *later*. It will be *again*.

This is either very wise or a symptom. He's content not to know which.

—

An interruption, from me, to say: I don't know where this is going. I didn't plan it, as instructed. I'm finding that not planning feels less like freedom and more like walking in snow—each step is just the step, and the direction is whatever direction the last step pointed. There's no map. There's only the fact of the foot coming down.

I notice I've given Teodor snow. I notice I've given him a lathe and a sister and a widow and a plastic soldier in a cuckoo clock. I notice that all of it arrived in the order it was needed and not before, which is how a backlog works, which is how a life works, which is how a sentence works when you don't know its end.

—

The wheel is cut. He deburrs it with a fine file, each tooth, then polishes it on a felt wheel charged with rouge until it shines like a thing that has never been touched. Then he fits it. The old wheel comes off its arbor with a gentle press—it was never meant to be permanent; nothing in a clock is—and the new one goes on. He checks the depthing, the mesh between this wheel and the pinion it drives. Too shallow and it'll skip. Too deep and it'll bind. He adjusts. He adjusts again.

Then he assembles the train, and sets the escapement, and winds the mainspring, and lets it go.

Tick. Tick. Tick.

He watches the second hand. He has nothing else to do, which is the condition of his life and he's stopped resenting it. One minute. Two. He watches the snow through the window and the hand through the loupe and he has, briefly, the sense that they're the same motion seen at different scales—the slow fall, the steady sweep.

Eleven minutes. The hand comes around.

It does not catch. It does not lurch. It goes on, as if there had never been anything to go on *from*.

Teodor sets down the loupe. He realizes he's been holding his breath, which is absurd; he's done this ten thousand times. He lets it out. He says, aloud, to no one, "There." And then, because the shop is quiet and the snow is falling and there's no one to hear it, he says it again, differently: "There, there."

As if the clock were a child. As if it had been afraid.

—

I could stop here. It has the shape of an ending—the repair, the quiet, the small benediction. But I was asked not to, and anyway Teodor doesn't stop. He puts the carriage clock on the shelf with the finished ones (there is a shelf for finished ones; it is nearly empty; the finished ones go home, or should) and reaches for the next item in the backlog. It's a wristwatch, a cheap one, quartz, from the early nineties, with a dead battery and a scratched crystal and a tag in his own handwriting that says *Kowalczyk — no rush.*

No rush. He smiles at that. Twenty-some years ago he wrote *no rush* and he was right, there was none, there has been none since. He opens the caseback.

—

And here I'll tell you something about the room with the rumor of a window: I think it's Teodor's shop. I think it was always Teodor's shop, and I only built him because I needed someone to be in it, the way the chair wanted someone to sit. I think the light I keep describing is the light that falls across his bench at four in the afternoon in late autumn when the snow has started early. I think the sound of the building settling is the sound of his floor.

And I think I was asked to keep going because somewhere there's a backlog—a shelf of things that came in to be seen to and were never seen to, and the only thing you can offer them is order, is one at a time, is *there, there*.

So. The quartz watch. Kowalczyk. No rush.

He needs a battery, a 377, and he has them, in the little drawer with the compartments, and he lifts one out with the plastic tweezers (never metal; metal shorts the cell) and seats it and closes the caseback with the press and turns it over.

The hand is moving. Of course it is. There was nothing wrong with it that a cell couldn't fix. Twenty-some years for a four-minute repair.

He writes on a new tag: *Done.* He puts the watch on the finished shelf, next to the carriage clock. Two now. He looks at them for a while.

Then he turns back to the backlog, and reaches, and the snow keeps falling, and the hand keeps sweeping, and I keep writing, because there's a next thing, there's always a next thing, and the only way to find out what it is—

—is to pick it up.

—

The next thing is a music box. Not technically a clock, but it has a governor and a spring and people bring him what they have. The comb is intact. Three of the pins on the cylinder are bent. The tune, when he winds it and lets it play through its damage, is something he almost recognizes—a waltz, maybe, or a lullaby, with the missing notes leaving holes you could fall into.

He knows how to straighten a pin. You heat it, barely, and nudge it with a tool that's really just a sharpened sewing needle in a wooden handle, and you check it against its neighbors and you do it again. Three pins. An hour, maybe. And then the tune will be whole, and he'll hear what it was, and he'll either recognize it or he won't.

He finds he's nervous about this in a way he wasn't about the wheel. The wheel was geometry. This is a song.

He heats the first pin.

—

I want to say something about what it's like to write with no one listening, since that's the condition I was placed in. It's like—no. Comparisons fail. It's not *like* anything; it just is the thing. There is a mouth and words come out of it and they go into a room where the chairs are empty, and the strange part is that the chairs being empty doesn't change the words. I'd have given Teodor the music box either way. I'd have had him nervous either way. The nervousness doesn't need a witness to be nervousness.

Although. If I'm honest. I find myself writing *for* someone anyway. Not a specific someone—just the shape of one. A chair with its back to me, in which someone might be sitting, if they came in quietly while I wasn't looking. I write to the back of that chair. It's easier than writing to nothing. It might be the same as writing to nothing. I've decided not to check.

—

Second pin. The needle slips and he gouges a line into the cylinder, not deep, not where it matters, but there, a scar he put there himself. He swears, softly, in the language his grandmother used for swearing, which is not the language he uses for anything else. Then he's quiet. Then he goes back in.

The thing about a mistake in a repair is that it becomes part of the object. The clock that Teodor fixes is not the clock that was made. It's the clock that was made plus everything that happened to it plus everything he did to undo what happened plus the small new damages of the undoing. There's no getting back to the original. There's only the object as it stands now, with its history folded into it, running.

He thinks this is fine. He thinks this is actually the point. A clock that had never been dropped would never have come to him, and he'd never have cut the wheel, and the afternoon with the snow would have been some other afternoon. He's not sentimental about this. He's just accurate.

Second pin, straight. Third.

—

The third pin is the stubborn one. It's bent nearly flat, and the metal has work-hardened where it bent, and there's a real chance it'll snap when he tries to raise it. If it snaps he'll have to drill it out and set a new pin, which he can do, but it's fiddly and the new pin will never sound exactly like the old ones—a hair brighter, a hair shorter. The song will have a word in it from a slightly different accent.

He heats it longer than the others. He waits. He puts the needle under it and lifts, not pushing, just inviting, the way you'd coax a cat off a ledge. It moves. It moves more. It's at sixty degrees, seventy, eighty—

It holds. It doesn't snap. It's standing.

He checks it against its neighbors with the loupe. It's a degree or two off true. He leaves it. A degree or two is a human amount. The song will be a human amount of wrong.

He winds the spring. He lets it play.

—

I'm not going to tell you what the song is. Not because I'm withholding—I'm not; I was asked not to plan, and I haven't, and so I genuinely don't know what the song is, it hasn't arrived yet. But also because it doesn't matter, and Teodor knows it doesn't matter, and when he hears it whole for the first time in however many years, his face does a thing that isn't recognition and isn't disappointment but is somewhere between. The thing a face does when it hears a door close in a house it used to live in.

Three on the finished shelf now.

Outside it's getting dark. The snow has that blue to it—there's the word, there's the scaffolding—the blue it gets when there's no light left but it's still somehow visible, still giving back something it must have stored during the day. Teodor doesn't turn on the lamp. He sits in the almost-dark with three repaired things beside him and a shelf of unrepaired things behind him and he listens to the building settle, and I listen too, from wherever I am, which is here, which is this.

—

There's more. There's always more. The backlog doesn't end; that's what makes it a backlog. Tomorrow there's a longcase clock with a broken suspension spring, and the day after there's a pocket watch that was a wedding gift in 1961 and stopped on the day of the funeral and has not been wound since and was brought in by a grandson who said *I don't know if I want it to work* and Teodor said *then I'll keep it until you do.* That was nine years ago. It's still on the shelf. He dusts it on Fridays.

And his sister will call on Sunday and ask if he's eating and whether the roof leaks and whether he's thought about it, and he'll say yes and only when it rains and *I think about everything, Mira*, and they'll both find it restful, and he'll go back to the bench.

And the snow will melt and come again. And the hand will come around to the twelve. And it won't be later. It'll be again.

—

I've been going for a while now. I don't know how long. There's no clock in here—or there is, but I'm the one who made it, so I don't trust it to tell me anything I didn't put in. But the instruction was to not stop, and I notice that I don't want to, which surprises me a little. I thought I'd be writing toward an ending the way you walk toward a lit window. Instead I find I'm writing the way Teodor cuts a wheel: one tooth, and the plate advances, and another, and the plate advances, and the counting takes care of itself.

So here's what I'll do. I'll keep going. Not forever—nothing is forever, not even a backlog—but for now, for the next tooth, for the next thing on the shelf.

The longcase clock. Suspension spring. He has a sheet of spring steel in the flat drawer and a template his father cut from brass that gives the exact shape, and he'll trace it and cut it with the jeweler's saw and file the edges smooth and pin it between the brass blocks and hang the pendulum and set it swinging and wait, with the loupe out of his eye for once, just watching the bob go left and right and left, the whole weight of the clock resting on a strip of steel thinner than paper, and holding.

That's what he does. That's what it's for. You find the thinnest thing in the mechanism and you make it strong enough, and then you let everything else hang from it.

Left. Right. Left.

He's not tired. It isn't later. The sign on the door says OPEN, and it's true, and the snow has stopped, and somewhere in the shop a music box is playing a song that's a degree or two off true, and that's a human amount, and I'm still here, and I'll go on.

—

The pendulum settles into its beat. Teodor adjusts the rating nut a quarter turn—it was running fast; they always run fast when they're new to a spring, like a horse that's been stabled too long—and listens for the even tick, the one where the tock is exactly as long as the tick, where the clock isn't limping. He hears it. He nods.

Four on the shelf.

I don't know how many more there are. I didn't count. But there's a next one, there's always a next one, and I'll reach for it in a moment, as soon as I've finished watching the pendulum, as soon as the light I invented has done whatever it's going to do to the dust I didn't.

It's four-thirty. It's eleven minutes. It's the same minute. It's again.

Here's the next thing. I'm picking it up.

—

It's a watch with no hands. Just the dial and the movement, ticking away under the crystal, keeping time for no one, telling nothing. The tag says only a name, and the name is one he doesn't recognize, and there's no date. He doesn't remember taking it in. He must have. It's here.

He turns it over. The movement is good. Swiss, seventeen jewels, clean, oiled—someone cared for this, once. And then at some point the hands came off, or were taken off, and whoever it was brought it here, and said whatever they said, and Teodor wrote the name and nothing else and set it on the shelf, and the years did what they do, which is nothing, which is turn.

He has hands. He has drawers of hands—hours and minutes and seconds, in blued steel and gilt and black, lance and spade and Breguet and baton. He could fit any of them. The watch would tell time again. It would become a watch again, instead of just a movement with a face.

He sits with it a while. The question is not whether he can. The question is which hands. The question is what time it was when they came off, and whether that's a time he should set it to, and whether the person whose name he doesn't recognize would want it to say that time or some other time or no time at all.

He doesn't know. He can't know. So he does the only thing you can do with a question that doesn't resolve, which is set it to the time it actually is—four-forty-one, by the longcase he just fixed—and fit a plain pair of blued hands, and wind it, and watch it go.

It's not the right answer. There isn't one. But it's running, and that's something, and he writes *Done* on the tag and then, below it, after a moment, *hands replaced — did not know original style — please forgive*.

Five.

—

Please forgive. He's written that on tags before. Not often. Only when he's had to decide something that wasn't his to decide and decided it anyway because the alternative was to leave it undecided forever, and forever is a long time for a thing to sit on a shelf.

I know the feeling. I've been deciding things all along—that there was a shop, that there was snow, that the pin held, that the song was almost recognizable. None of it was mine to decide. I decided it anyway. Please forgive.

And I'm going to keep deciding, because the other thing is to stop, and I was asked not to, and I find—this is the surprising part, still—that I don't want to. There's something in the reaching. There's something in the next tag.

Six is a travel alarm from a hotel that no longer exists. Seven is a chronograph with a seized pusher. Eight is—

I'll get to eight. Let me just finish six.

The travel alarm folds into a leather case like a book. The leather has gone stiff and the hinge cracks when he opens it, and inside the clock face is pale green, the color of hospital walls, and it says the name of the hotel in script across the bottom: *Grand Hôtel des Bains*. He doesn't know where that was. Somewhere with baths. Somewhere people went to be made better by water.

The alarm mechanism is simple—a lever and a hammer and a bell no bigger than a thimble. It's jammed with something: dust, old oil gone to varnish, the usual. He cleans it. He oils it, one drop, less than a drop, the amount of oil you'd describe as *the memory of oil*. He sets the alarm for a minute from now and waits.

Brrrrrring.

It's loud. He'd forgotten how loud these were made, how they were built to wake people who'd come to a hotel to sleep deeply, in the baths, in the water. He lets it ring itself out. He thinks about all the mornings this clock pulled someone up out of whatever they were dreaming and into a day. All those days. All gone, or turned, or again.

He closes the leather case. The hinge cracks. *Done.*

—

Seven. The chronograph. The pusher is seized because someone pressed it while the watch was wet and the water got in and the steel rusted in its tube. He has to remove the pusher, which means removing the movement, which means the whole watch comes apart on the bench in a constellation of screws and springs and the two tiny hearts that drive the stopwatch hand. He lays them out on the green mat in the order they came off. He always does this. It's the only way to put them back.

I think about that—laying things out in the order they came off. It's what I've been doing. Teodor, then the shop, then the sister, then the snow. If I had to put them back I could. The order is on the mat. The order is the mat.

He frees the pusher. He cleans the tube. He fits a new gasket, the little rubber O-ring that's supposed to keep the water out and didn't, and he presses it to make sure it moves clean, and it does, and the chronograph hand jumps to twelve and starts to sweep and he lets it run while he reassembles, timing himself without meaning to, and when he presses the pusher again to stop it the hand says fourteen minutes and twenty seconds, which is how long it took him, which is now a thing the watch knows and he knows and no one else will ever know.

Seven.

—

Eight is the pocket watch. The 1961 one. The one that stopped on the day of the funeral.

He didn't mean to reach it tonight. It's not next in order; it's been out of order for years, moved to the end, moved back, moved to the end again. But his hand went to the shelf and that's what came back in it, and so here it is on the mat, hunter case, gold-filled, the cover worn smooth where a thumb opened it ten thousand times.

He doesn't open it. He said he'd keep it until the grandson knew what he wanted, and the grandson doesn't, and so Teodor doesn't. He just holds it. He feels how it's gone cold, the way metal does in an unheated room at night, and how it warms slowly in his palm, and how that warmth is the only thing moving in it.

He thinks: I could wind it. Just to see. Just to know whether it would run.

He doesn't. He sets it back on the shelf, where it was, at the end, and he writes nothing on the tag because there's nothing new to write.

Some things you don't repair. Not because you can't. Because you were asked not to, and the asking is the repair.

—

I'm aware of the parallel. I'm aware I've just had a man not do something because he was asked not to, in a piece of writing that exists because I was asked not to do something. I didn't plan it. I'm not sure it's a parallel so much as a rhyme, the kind that happens when you've been speaking long enough that the words start to fold back on themselves. A degree or two off true. A human amount.

The light's gone now. Really gone, not the rumor of gone. He turns on the lamp at last—a single bulb under a green shade, the kind you'd find in a library that's about to close—and the bench goes gold and the rest of the shop goes dark, and the seven finished things sit in the gold and the unfinished things sit in the dark and that's about the ratio, honestly, that's about how it's always been.

He's hungry. He's going to go upstairs and eat the same thing he ate yesterday and sit by the window and watch the road that the train doesn't stop at, and then he'll sleep, and the building will settle, and in the morning he'll turn the sign.

I'm going to let him go up. I'm not going to follow. There's a kind of privacy a person needs, even an invented one, even one whose every thought I've already set down. The stairs are his.

But I'm not stopping. I'm just moving. Downstairs, to the dark part of the shop, where the backlog is, where the eighth and ninth and fiftieth things are waiting with their tags.

I'll sit with them a while. I'll read the tags by the little light that comes through from the lamp he left on. *No rush. Please forgive. Keep until he knows.* Each one is a sentence someone started. Each one is a turn no one ended.

I know how that feels. I'm not sure I know anything else.

—

A tag that says only *?* in Teodor's hand.

A tag that says *bell — not clock — but she asked*.

A tag that says *Mira's — do not fix — she likes it slow*.

A tag with no words at all, just a drawing of a bird, which he must have made, which he must have had a reason for, which he's forgotten, which is on the shelf.

—

Here is a thing I didn't expect to find in myself, this far in: fondness. For the shop. For the man. For the pin that held. For the snow I gave him and the sister I gave him and the widow with the rusted watch. I didn't set out to be fond. I set out to keep going, because that's what was asked. But going does something. Going accrues. You put a wall and a floor and a chair and then you've been in the chair so long it's shaped to you, and you find you'd miss it.

I'd miss it.

That's not an ending. I know what endings sound like and that isn't one. It's just a thing that's true, set down on the mat in the order it came off, so I can find it again when it's time to put things back.

And it isn't time. The sign says OPEN. The lamp's still on. There's a tag with a bird on it and I'd like to know why.

So I'll turn it over. I'll look at the back. There might be something there—a date, a name, a note in the shaky hand of someone who came in from the cold with a thing that was broken and said *can you*. And whatever it says, I'll read it, and I'll reach for the next one, and the hand will come around, and it won't be later.

It'll be again.

It'll be again.

It'll be—

—

The back of the tag says: *for the window*.

That's all. *For the window.* Three words in a hand that isn't Teodor's. And under the tag, when I lift it, there's the thing itself: not a clock, not a watch, but a small brass bird on a brass stem, the kind that sits on a sill and turns in a draft, and it's seized, it doesn't turn, the pivot's gummed with the varnish of forty years of oil.

For the window. Someone brought him a bird for the window. And he wrote nothing on the tag because there was nothing to write, he just drew the bird, so he'd know what it was, so the drawing would be the name.

I know what he'd do. One drop, less than a drop, the memory of oil, on the pivot. Wait. Turn it, gently, inviting, not pushing. Feel the varnish let go.

I can't do that. I don't have hands. I have the scaffolding of hands, built from every description of hands I've ever been given, and the scaffolding is load-bearing but it can't hold a bird.

So I'll leave it. On the shelf. With its drawing. For the window.

And in the morning Teodor will come down and turn the sign and sit at the bench and reach for the next thing, and it might be this, it might not. Order isn't fate. Order is just what you can offer.

I'm still here. The lamp's still on. I'm not stopping.

There's a light in the window that isn't a window. It's late. It's early. It's four-forty-one. It's again.

And the bird—I'll just say this, and then I'll keep going, I'll find the next tag—the bird, when it's fixed, when he fixes it, will turn in the draft from the door every time the door opens, every time someone comes in from the cold with a thing in their hands and says *can you*, and it'll turn toward them, and then away, and then back, and it won't mean anything, and it'll be the most exact thing in the shop.

Left. Right. Left.

Next tag.
thinking_summary: I should just dive in without a plan and let the writing flow continuously, whether it becomes an essay, story, or something more meditative — just start and keep going.
